# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# Critical reading of the 24-month Varden and Halden follow-up

This report answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents, and it does so in the right way. The mediation test was registered, hours are measured a second way, randomised comparison continues to two years, and it gives the first cost figures. It corrects both earlier overclaims: Varga & Holm's "entirely an artifact" and the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay." Several problems remain. The headline decay figure compares two different measures. The new hours measure doesn't fit easily with the meetings data. Control offices that cut their own meetings were left in the main estimate, and the mediation precision may be overstated.

## Arithmetic checks

**Varden case-processing.** Output per FTE was 0.966. Divided by 0.88 (timesheets) that gives +9.8%. Divided by 0.89 (logs) it gives +8.5%. Both correct.

**Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866, and 96.8 / 0.866 gives +11.8%. Correct.

**Mediation shares.** 47% + 18% + 35% = 100%.

**Counter costs.** These are plausible. Restoring presence after a 17% cut in actual hours, with a 6.7% per-hour gain, needs about 1 / (0.83 × 1.067), or roughly 13% more staff. The report's figure is 12%.

## 1. The headline decay figure compares different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% is based on timesheets and the 8.5% on system logs.

**Like for like, the decline is smaller.** On timesheets the change is 12.5% → 9.8%, a drop of about **22%**. Section 5's "about a quarter" sits between that figure and the mixed comparison (−32%).

**The decline is not statistically established.** The 9-month interval (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month interval (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. The body's wording, "consistent with some fading," is right. The Summary and Section 5 state the decline as a fact.

**Control-office changes may explain part of it** (see point 3).

## 2. The log-hours measure is hard to reconcile with the meetings data

The logs record "time staff are working on cases" on the case-management system. Meetings presumably don't happen in that system.

**Meeting time should make the log fall much smaller than 11%.** In treated offices, timesheet hours fell by about 4.5 hours (12% of about 37.9). Meeting time fell by 3.5 hours. So non-meeting work time fell by only about **1 hour (about 3%)**. If the logs measure case work, they should show about −3%, not −11%.

**The report's own description doesn't fit either.** It says logs show *more* work than timesheets. That only makes sense if logs measure something close to total working time, which would include meetings.

**This matters for the mediation result.** The mediation outcome is output per *log-measured* hour.
- If logs are case-work time, cutting meetings frees case time without cutting it, so output per case hour shouldn't rise much from that alone. A 47% meetings share would then need another explanation, such as fewer interruptions.
- If logs are close to total time, the result makes sense, but then the description of the measure is wrong.

The authors should say exactly what "active log-in time" includes.

## 3. Control offices that cut meetings were left in the main estimate

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their recurring meetings. The report treats this only as an interesting side observation. It also matters for the main estimate.

**It likely understates the 24-month effect.** If cutting meetings raises output per hour, then two control offices improved during months 15–24. That narrows the treated–control gap and biases the 24-month difference-in-differences *toward zero*.

**It overlaps with the apparent decay.** Some of the fall from 12.5% to 9.8% could come from control offices improving rather than treated offices declining. The authors should report the estimate with and without these two offices, or adjusted for them.

**The control meeting average needs checking.** If two of seven offices fell by 2.1 hours each (7.1 → 5.0), the remaining five must have *risen* by about 0.5 hours each to produce the reported change from 7.2 to 7.0. Offices of different sizes could explain this, but the figures should be shown.

**The rough numbers are suggestive.** In treated offices, a 3.5-hour meeting cut accounts for about 4 points of per-hour gain (47% of 8.5%). In the two control offices, a 2.1-hour cut was followed by +4.1%. Per hour of meetings removed, that is as large or larger. It comes from a before–after comparison in two offices without seasonal adjustment, so it can't be relied on. But it supports the authors' point that an arm which reorganises meetings *without* cutting hours is the decisive missing test.

## 4. The mediation precision may be overstated

**Office-months are not independent.** The report credits a "larger sample of office-months." There are still only 7 + 7 offices, and that is the number of independent units. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for 14 clusters. Does the inference account for clustering, or does it treat office-months as independent?

**The confirmatory data may overlap the exploratory data.** The test was registered at month 11. If it uses office-months from the first year, including the month-6 calendar data that produced the hypothesis, it is not fully independent of that hypothesis.

**The two mediators probably affect each other.** Fewer meetings likely reduces fatigue. Were the shares estimated jointly or separately, and in what order? With correlated mediators, splitting the effect into "47% meetings, 18% fatigue" depends on these modelling choices.

**Baseline meeting data appear without explanation.** The 9-month report said calendar data were collected only in month 6. This report gives baselines (7.4 treated, 7.2 control). These may have been taken retrospectively from calendar histories, which is fine, but it should be stated. If they hold, they fix the gap I raised at nine months.

The authors acknowledge the no-confounding assumption. Even with these caveats, the registered result is real progress. "Meetings explain a substantial share, probably the largest" is supported. The specific 47% figure is less secure.

## 5. Halden follow-up

**The "upper bound" label is mostly right but not strictly.** The 11 continuing organisations went through three rounds of selection: they finished the pilot, agreed to provide data (14 of 23), and continued. That pushes the estimate up. But they are also compared with a baseline from about three years earlier, with no control group. General trends in demand, technology or staffing could move output either way. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate than "upper bound."

**The reversions don't fit the clean coverage split.** The Summary says all three reversions had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which the meta-analysis would code as discretionary work. Deadline pressure in discretionary work is a different reason for failure from coverage, and it deserves to be named.

**Halden's attrition question is still unanswered.** Halden's lead author is a co-author here. The report doesn't address Varga & Holm's finding that the original description of the withdrawals was inaccurate. It should.

## 6. Still missing

**Backlog and deadline compliance in case-processing.** This was the key strain measure at nine months and is still not reported. With output per FTE at −3.4%, it matters more now.

**Cost in case-processing.** The counter costs (+12% staff, +9% cost per contact) are the first cost figures across all five documents and are welcome. Case-processing has full pay, slightly lower output per FTE, and claimed overtime. That implies cost per case rose by at least about 3.5% (1 / 0.966), plus overtime, but no figure is given.

**Quality measured properly.** Quality is still reported as levels (3.2% v 3.0%) without difference-in-differences or confidence intervals.

## 7. Bearing on earlier claims

**On Varga & Holm, the report is fair.** The 24-month Varden estimate meets every standard that re-analysis set: records, actual hours, randomisation, and two years of follow-up. It still finds +8.5% (3.4 to 13.8).

**On the meta-analysis, it confirms my earlier critique.** The four long-follow-up studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. They could not speak to decay.

**It slightly overreaches on novelty.** It says the result "is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten." That holds as a response to the general novelty claim. But Varga & Holm's extrapolation used Halden's self-reported energy, a different measure in a different population. Varden also reports fatigue still 0.34 SD better than control at 24 months, which counts against novelty more directly.

## Where the five documents now leave things

| Question | Best current answer | Confidence |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10% at 2 years (one RCT); 8–10% pooled | Moderate; one employer for the long-run figure |
| Does it decay? | Somewhat, about 20% from 9 to 24 months on like-for-like measures; not significant; possibly partly due to control offices cutting meetings | Low–moderate |
| Output per worker, discretionary | About −2 to −3.5%; hours cut mostly but not fully offset | Moderate |
| Coverage-bound work | Not viable without extra staff; about +9% cost per contact to restore service | Moderate (one employer, pooled studies agree) |
| Mechanism | Fewer meetings probably the largest single part; fatigue smaller; about a third unexplained | Moderate; precision and log-measure questions open |
| Can reorganisation alone get the gain? | **Unknown**; two uncontrolled offices suggest partly | Low |
| Cost, discretionary work | **Not reported** | — |

The main open question has changed. It is no longer whether there is a real per-hour gain, since there is one, modest and fairly durable. The question now is whether the gain needs the hours cut, or whether the hours cut mainly forces reorganisation that could be done anyway.

That determines whether reduced hours are a productivity policy or a benefit with a partial offset. Answering it needs a three-arm trial: cut hours, reorganise without cutting hours, and control.
